utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Merovci.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The cross-examination by Mr. O'Sullivan will continue in a moment, and that will be followed by cross-examination by other counsel. I remind you that the solemn declaration to speak the truth which you made at the beginning of your evidence continues to apply throughout your evidence. Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Merovci.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I'd like to begin this morning by asking you a question or two about Zoran Andjelkovic. Now, you know that he was the head of the Provisional Executive Council for Kosovo and Metohija; correct?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were institutions that were for us irrelevant at the time; and to tell you the truth, I don't know what positions such people had accurately.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Did you know that this body had been created by the Government of Serbia in autumn 1998?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: You must understand that we did not agree with such -- did not accept such bodies, and we simply ignored them. By saying that, I personally didn't -- was not familiar with such people, such bodies, and their positions in them according to the hierarchy of the regime then.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: But you are aware that this body existed and that Mr. Andjelkovic was a part of it. You know it existed and you know who he was; you know that much, don't you?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I do know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Now, on the 28th of April, 1999, you've testified about the meeting held in the provincial government building in Pristina, and you, Dr. Rugova, Mr. Milutinovic, Mr. Sainovic, Professor Markovic, and Mr. Andjelkovic were present. Do you recall testifying about that?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. I testified, but I must be specific about my role because my presence was required at such meetings in my capacity as a technical person, because as I said that was a role I played during all my time I served with Mr. Rugova. Therefore, my presence there was a necessity for me to be by his side, but I didn't have any responsibility because, as I said, I was simply a technical person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Merovci, you've explained that to us yesterday. You are anxious that we should make progress with the case. If you continue to be so defensive in your answers, always wanting to add an explanation that we've already heard before, then we will be here much longer than today. It's important that you just listen to the question that's asked and try to answer the particular point that counsel's making. He's not trying to catch you out or trip you up in the way that he's presenting these questions. I'm not saying that counsel don't do that, sometimes they will do that, but that's clearly not what Mr. O'Sullivan's doing. So please try to answer the particular question that's put to you. Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Do you recall that at the beginning of this meeting, that Dr. Rugova presented Mr. Milutinovic with a gift of one of his precious stones, the ones he would offer as a symbolic representation of the riches of Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall this incident particularly, but if I am not mistaken this -- such a stone was given to Mr. Milosevic on our occasion before going to Rome.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Can I have Exhibit P416 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Mr. Merovci, in front of you, you should have the joint statement that was signed by Dr. Rugova and Mr. Milutinovic on the 28th of April. You looked at it yesterday in court. I want to look at it very briefly with you. You'll see in paragraph 4 of this document reference is made to the Provisional Executive Council of Kosovo and Metohija, of which Mr. Andjelkovic, I submit, was the head. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And in that same paragraph, paragraph 4, there's a reference to the basic document on self-government in Kosovo and Metohija, and yesterday I suggested to you that Professor Markovic was the head of both the delegation that existed in 1998 and the Rambouillet delegation; correct?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Now, you'll see that paragraph 1 talks about, and I quote: "It is necessary to immediately renew and intensify discussions ..." You'll see that paragraph 2 talks about having direct talks involving all communities living in Kosovo based on mutual trust and finding a way out of the current situation. Paragraph 3 talks about participation of the international community. And, more generally, paragraph 4 contemplates an immediate but temporary way out of the current situation through this Executive Council body. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Now, at the end of the meeting, you know that Mr. Milutinovic and Dr. Rugova gave statements to the press; correct?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And there were both domestic and international journalists who were present; correct?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that there were journalists, but I don't recall that there were foreign journalists.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, Exhibit 1D60 is a video-clip which I'd like to play. It contains footage of the meeting itself and statements made by Mr. Milutinovic and Dr. Rugova. I'll ask that the video start. Let's make sure that it's on the screen for Mr. Merovci. Are we set for Mr. Merovci. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Can we stop there, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: In that frame, we see the six of you sitting in the room; and facing the camera at the far end is Mr. Milutinovic and to his right is Dr. Rugova, and you are sitting to the right of Dr. Rugova; correct?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Can we continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Can we stop, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: That's Mr. Andjelkovic we see on the screen?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Can we continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Can we stop there.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Looking at the screen, the man on the left with the moustache is Mr. Sainovic and to his left is Professor Markovic; correct?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, when the tape continues, there will be the text of -- Mr. Milutinovic and Dr. Rugova giving their statements. The interpreters have been provided with a transcript to facilitate interpretation. The speakers are speaking Serbian. Can we continue.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Mr. Milutinovic: I believe that Mr. Rugova and I have talked for the second time, and like you know on several meetings before that we've had starting with the one in Belgrade between President Milosevic and Dr. Rugova. Today we have agreed on joint statement which we'll be giving to you later on, in which we have pointed out the necessity of renewal of the talks between the Republic of Serbia government and political leaders and Albanian political leaders in Kosovo and Metohija on political agreement under which Kosovo will be given wide self-governance with full respect of equality between all the citizens and all the communities as well as the sovereignty and territory integrity of Serbia and Yugoslavia. We have considered this approach for basis and lasting right of the problem in Kosovo. We have both concluded that talks shall be direct with equal participation of all the national communities that reside in Kosovo and Metohija and that such talks should be direct -- that should be a direct approval of stronger mutual trust which is a vital condition for getting out of the present situation. "We have agreed as well that on the basis of our mutual agreement in the role of guest of the international community should be present. And lastly, under item 4, we have agreed on the necessity of temporary and alter conditions in which the temporary Executive Council should be functioning until the establishment of the bodies which have been provided for in the agreement, of which we will talk. This is the essence of today's talks. We have concluded that the bombing and the aggression on our country should be put to a stop as soon as possible. We think that the international community will today and from this place adopt our appeal and that this should be a precondition for the people to come back to their homes and start a normal life in all the national communities and surroundings because of the simplest reason and that is without common life of all the national communities there is no lasting peace in the area. "Dr. Rugova: This situation, the most important thing is that we have established mutual -- more mutual trust even though we had it even earlier while we were on agreement on Kosova, so we had trust now and in last context in Belgrade with Milosevic, Milutinovic, and Sainovic as vice-president of the government, so we have made it to cooperate it, of course is that we will continue to achieve the solution for Kosova and our main goal is to get out of this present situation. "We will intend to form the bodies in Kosova, the Kosova institutions that will be for the nationalities and for the citizens of Kosova and what is more important, we have established new trust and greater trust which the world will appreciate as well."

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I ask that the transcript reflect that beginning at page 7, line 5, Dr. Rugova is speaking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Mr. Merovci, you heard what Mr. Rugova spoke of, he spoke of new trust and greater trust, cooperation to achieve a solution for Kosovo, getting out of the current situation, and forming new bodies for all nationalities and all citizens of Kosovo. Now, isn't what Dr. Rugova said there entirely consistent with the guiding principles of his political life?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is leading question. I don't know what you -- what your question is. What he said was heard by all. I don't know what your question is. Can you be more explicit about it so that we can be brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yes. The words that Mr. Rugova spoke, about finding a solution, ending the situation, improving the life of all citizens in Kosovo, greater trust to cooperation, those are the principles that from the time Mr. Rugova started in the LDK in the late 1980s was the basis of his political platforms and political life?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is true. But if we look at the entire text, even though we didn't hear the entire text, what it says about the international community being present in the meeting simply as guests is not what Mr. Rugova said. It's contrary to his wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Merovci, what was actually going on at this stage that we've viewed on the video? We've seen that everyone was meeting, and it's not uncommon at political meetings for a picture or a film to be taken to show the public that everyone is talking, in spite of the fact that they're shaking hands they're probably gritting their teeth and forcing a smile. So that's not an unusual event, but then we hear the words that the participants utter. Now, what was Mr. Rugova actually doing at that stage? This is where I think we need to hear more from you because it puts a completely different gloss on that meeting from the one that appears in your statement in paragraph 72.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was a meeting like all other meetings. But as I said in my statements, we considered being detained at home, being under house arrest and a tendency -- we saw tendencies to manipulate Mr. Rugova. For us, it was, as I said, a life-and-death struggle, and what I am saying now is proven by later developments. Such initiatives were -- were staged, in our view, because otherwise why didn't they continue to abide by the same approach? As you asked me about Mr. Rugova, I may tell you that he was an isolated man in a difficult psychological and physical situation, and he was thinking only of saving his life. I think this is more or less the crux of the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you wish to ask anything further, Mr. O'Sullivan? Thank you. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Merovci, good morning. I'm Toma Fila and I represent Nikola Sainovic. I see you have your statement before you. I don't have any questions, actually. I just need some clarifications. We resided in the same country, but some people did not in -- reside in that country; that's why the clarifications are necessary. In paragraph 8, you're speaking about a decision on the ban to sell property by Serbs and the programme that was posed by us and Ante Markovic, the prime minister at the time. This was done during the period of the SFRY, and Ante Markovic was a Croat, who was the prime minister at the time, is that correct, and I'm talking about the year 1988?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The law we are talking about was dated earlier; it was dictated on us by the Serb regime.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In 1988, the former Yugoslavia still existed, isn't that correct? Do you remember that? In 1988, this was still the time of the SFRY?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, you may put it that way. But following 1986, after the event of Mr. Milosevic took power, such measures were imposed which banned the sale of property by the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: We will come to that. I just want to make a distinction. I don't have many objections to what you've said; I just want to make a few clarifications. So up to 1991, the state in place was the SFRY; after that, was the FRY; and now it is the SR Serbia. The law that you've mentioned, would you agree with me that this was not the law on the ban of sale but on limited sale but all non-Albanians; and if you remember it well, the sale could have been allowed with the provision that there should have been a prior approval by the ministry. Wouldn't that be correct? If you don't remember, it doesn't matter.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember very well. And if you can prove a single case that the ministry has given its prior approval, I will withdraw what I said. This was not allowed, and that happened to me personally. A Serb asked me to sell his house to me and this was a private enterprise, but it was impossible to do that. And this is a fact. There is documentation to prove what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Very well. There were instances where this was allowed but this was not my question. What I was saying was this applied to all non-Albanians, not only Serbs, but this was not a full ban but a limitation. You're saying that in this way Albanians were discriminated against. How can you say that Albanians were discriminated against if the Serbs were prohibited from selling their property? Wouldn't that be discrimination against the Serbs and there the law was broken on many occasions and there was severe penalty for that. Would -- don't you remember that? I believe that this was discrimination against the Serbs because the Serbs were affected; they were the ones who couldn't sell their property?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I object that's a compound question, and also I think the evidence was Serbs were not allowed to sell to Albanians or non-Serbs. They were allowed to sell to Serbs apparently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Fila, there may be a mistake in the transcript in the transcript at page 10 on line 10, the limited sale was to non-Serbs, I think you must have meant to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Non-Serbs were limited in sales to Albanians, not -- it didn't apply in the transactions between Albanians because there are Turks and Roma there as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because under that law --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, just a moment. You tell me what you say the law was. Was it preventing Serbs from selling to any non-Serb without prior approval, or was it simply preventing sales to Albanians without prior approval?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The latter is the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So a Serb could have sold his property to any other nationality but an Albanian -- any other ethnic group but an Albanian?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the contrary. Under the law, approval should have been sought by anybody who wanted to sell property, not only by Serbs or Albanians. And approvals were given for any Serbs selling to another Serb, and you're right there, sir; however, under the law there was a restriction on the sale of property. And it was not specifically mentioned what ethnicity was in question. Every time you wished to sell, you had to obtain prior approval.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Merovci, what Mr. Fila is suggesting that there wasn't a law that said, You will not sell to Albanians; the law required administrative approval before you could sell to anyone and that in practice I think what you're saying -- do you agree with that, first of all, that it was necessary to get approval to sell to anyone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was a political decision, first and foremost, and it was described as discriminatory by all organisations. In real terms, this -- to answer your question, Your Honour, in real terms it operated like this. It was forbidden to sell solid properties in the case of the buyers being Albanians; and in order for the transaction to take place, of course it have -- you have to get -- obtain a prior approval in Belgrade. I don't recall of anyone managing to get that approval; then agencies and Serbs appeared who could be corrupted and maybe in some instances could obtain such approval. But still, there were other difficulties to overcome and the transaction never -- was never effected. It was a discriminating law, both against Albanians' and Serbs' interests. It is discriminating both ways, to sell and to buy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And can I take it that the law required approval, even for a Serb to sell to another Serb; but in practice, it was easier to get approval for such a transaction?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot say that. I cannot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, the second matter that Mr. Fila raised was the question -- he's put to you the proposition that it was also discriminating against Serbs because it restricted the market for their property. Now, I think in your earlier evidence you've already agreed with that. You've already said that to the Prosecutor in the course of the evidence, that there was an element of discrimination against Serbs in this law as well. So we can move beyond that, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Finally, in order to bring this to an end, do you believe that the reason for passing these reasons, or rather, a political explanation was to prevent the Serbs from moving out of Kosovo? Was that the reason that was given? Wasn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I say yes, then I would accept the logic of the Serbs moving from Kosova, but I do not accept this logic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So I did not ask you whether that was right; I just wanted to remind you that the explanation that was given publicly for that law was to prevent the Serbs from moving out. I'm not saying that that was the case, but that was the explanation given by the state for this happening. Did you hear that kind of explanation? That's what I'm asking you. I'm not asking you to say that the explanation is right, but was that the explanation that was given?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now I would like to ask you to look at paragraph 12. Mr. Merovci, I highly appreciate the fact that you're in a hurry. I'm a businessman myself. So, please, let us keep your answers short and my questions short so that you get home as soon as possible. In paragraph 12, at the end of your statement, you say that if a kind of confederation is to be established, Kosovo should have an opportunity to choose who they're going to live with. I'm just asking you what you meant by that -- that last sentence in paragraph 12. That is it. Kosovo should be able to choose with whom it would associate. What does that mean, with whom it would associate? Please look at your statement.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot see the paragraph on the screen; however, I can give you an explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: All right. You don't even have to see it. You should have the statement in your hands; that's the problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you have a copy of your statement there? No?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't have it before me now.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Merovci, I have it in Serbian, if that's any good for you.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just read out in B/C/S that sentence, and it will be okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I can give it to you in Serbian. You want to have a look? It's my own copy, so it's been marked on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's okay. Mr. Hannis has a spare copy which he's about to pass over to, and if you can turn to paragraph 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I have both English and B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] .

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Paragraph 12, the last sentence, it says Kosovo and so on and so forth. Can you just explain what it was that you were trying to say.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was part of the platform of the LDK and of all political associations of the Albanians in the Balkans in addition to Albania; so Montenegro, southern Serbia, and part of Macedonia. There were three options. If Yugoslavia remained as it was with the existing bordering, then Kosova should enjoy the status of a republic. If independent states were to be created within Yugoslavia, then Kosova wants full independence. However, if the external borders are effected in any way, the Albanians should choose whom they would associate with. This was the context. This was a public platform that was emphasised by Mr. Rugova as well while he testified here.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: My question is: What does that mean they should be able to choose with whom they would associate? They don't have to be with Yugoslavia. They can be with Albania, Macedonia, Montenegro, whatever. I want you to explain what this option means. Can they unite with Albania, for instance? Is that the option? That's why I don't understand what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you are asking I've already answered that, but I will repeat it. The last version was if the external borders are changed, the Helsinki charter, then the Albanians in the former Yugoslavia, their right of associating with whomever they want to should be recognized. This is what I said. There was no prejudice whether it would be Albania, Macedonia, Bulgaria. This was the thought prevailing in the platform and in this statement of mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: But those were the options, right? Albania, Macedonia, Yugoslavia, right? That's what you were trying to say, right?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could have been Italy as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: All right. Now there's paragraph 13. In paragraph 13, you use certain terms. So you say that after the autonomy in Kosovo was abolished, emergency measures were introduced, or rather, effectively martial law you say. And what kind of emergency measures? What are you saying about 1989? Have you seen your own statement? Perhaps the translation is not good, so that's why it's better for you to see what it says. So you say emergency measures and martial law so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let's stop there. This statement, presumably, can be brought up on e-court in Albanian and --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is not an Albanian translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There isn't one at all?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Even though the Albanian language was used in the interview?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I see that's what it says. I would have to address that with the witness, but all we have are a B/C/S and an English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Merovci, I take it now has a B/C/S version. Is that what you gave him, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I gave him the English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, he should also have the B/C/S copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We have that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please pass that to him. Mr. Merovci, I think you may be more comfortable with this one; and if you turn to page 13, I think you and Mr. Fila will be on the same wavelength. Carry on, please, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Paragraph 13.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your question is clear. I have given this statement in English because I understood everything that was said during the interview.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: If the witness could repeat this part, please, the interpreter didn't catch it, sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Kosovo institutions had all the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: A part of what you said was not picked up by the interpreter. Could you repeat what you've just said, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When the autonomy was revoked by force and before the constitutional changes that were imposed by the use of force, all the institutions in Kosova were under emergency and coercive measures. Some institutions as, for example, the financial ones had to go through the process of liquidation, which was imposed on them. And this process was not in favour of the Albanians because it resulted in them remaining without jobs.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You answered to part of what my question was, but I'm interested in the term you use here; "emergency measures and a state of war." How can you talk about a state of war in 1989? And there were these financial measures, but we'll get to that. Or did you just say this by way of a description? I mean, we really need an explanation why you said a state of war in Kosovo and emergency measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the word "state of war" I don't think appear in the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But it says so here in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And when I say "English translation," in fact it should be "English original" because that's the language that was used to give the statement. So it would appear to be some difficulty with the B/C/S translation. The part that I'm looking at says: "It was introduced that the Albanian workers had to wear new identity badges which had the term literally translated 'violently installed organs" printed on them. They said that if the Albanians wore these badges, it would indicated that they accepted the imposition of emergency measures and thus the dominance of the Serbs."

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The sentence I'm reading is the one before that it reads as follows: "After the abrogation of autonomy, emergency measures had been imposed on Kosovo, effectively a state of war, martial law." That is the English version and that's what I'm reading out in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But martial law does not mean a state of war. Martial law means military rule. It doesn't mean an ongoing conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let him explain then what kind of military rule was established in 1989, because that wasn't the case either.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Or did you just want to say this by way of a description? Because this is a time when the SFRY was still in existence, right?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please tell me which paragraph and which sentence it is exactly, because I can't find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Paragraph 13, and the sentence reads as follows; that is 2, 4, 6, 7, line 7 of paragraph 13. Have you found it? And the sentence reads as follows: "After the abrogation of autonomy," I'm reminding you of the fact that you're talking about 1989, "emergency measures had been imposed on Kosovo, effectively a state of war," it says in Serbian; whereas, in English it says "effectively martial law." Can you please explain to us what it is you meant by this.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a misinterpretation or a mistranslation. This is the first time I'm looking at the B/C/S version. I have written it in English. As the Judge explained it, that's the way it is. But I will explain it here. Kosovo was in a military state and did not -- in a state of war. This is the misinterpretation and the relevant version is the one I signed. Kosovo was then full of tanks and military equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In 1989? Is that what you're saying? Paragraph 13 refers to 1989, not 1999. You'd be right as far as 1999 is concerned, but here you're talking about 1989. Have you made a mistake in terms of time? This is the time of the SFRY; that's why I'm asking you about this. What kind of military rule in 1989? You worked in a bank at that time, remember?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're now prejudicing what I said. I'll tell you again. I did not say it was a state of war. There were emergency measures which reflected on the population as a military state. This is the truth, and you're prejudicing what I said. I'm telling you, I did not say "state of war," and you're saying, Yes, you did. I said "a military state," and I did not put this military state in quotation marks. The extraordinary measures were emergency measures were under quotation marks. The military state was proven by the military presence in Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: It was full of tanks and weapons in 1989. That is what you claim, if I understood you correctly, and that it was military rule, right, ten years before the conflict broke out? And at the time of the SFRY. That is what you're claiming now, if I understood you well. Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot answer it with yes or no before I tell you that the constitutional changes in Kosova were carried out by force. And the entire world knows this, and all the international organisations that were present there know this.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Sir, I repeat, a few moments ago you said that it was full of tanks, weapons, that there were lots of troops, there was military rule in Kosovo. You said that two minutes ago. Don't make me read the transcript. Are you claiming to us now that in 1989 there was military rule in Kosovo, that laws of war were in force? Is that what you're claiming right now, yes or no? And then let's move on if that's your answer.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that there were a state of war or war rule. These were emergency measures; this is what I said. There were tanks and heavy equipment on the streets in Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Let's read it out yet again. Oh, all right. You said what you said. It doesn't work. So this is the time of social ownership and social property, right, 1989? That is what prevailed throughout Yugoslavia, right? Were emergency measures introduced then when companies were being liquidated? So that was the term used. It wasn't violent measures, as you say. When a company went under receivership, then there were these measures that were introduced. So this was done in the case of socially owned property, right? And then there would be receivership authority, the Workers' Council would not be in existence any longer, that was the way things were done. Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object. There are three or four questions there. I'm not sure which one he's supposed to answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Fila, if you wish this to be productive, you need to get an answer to each part of the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: All right. Was there social ownership at that time, in 1989, as the basic form of ownership?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Were companies socially owned?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Let the record reflect that he said "yes" a few moments ago as well, because it is not in the transcript. Now, when this socially owned enterprise company was liquidated, then these emergency or receivership measures were introduced. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am an engineer and you are a lawyer. I'm sorry that you are mixing up these things. The extraordinary emergency measures were introduced before liquidation, and they were applied to all institutions, not simply to the financial institutions. I gave you the example of a financial institution because I worked there, but you can say this of schools, of associations, of kindergartens, of creches, of libraries, of any other organisation. All of them were subjected to extraordinary measures, and the procedure of liquidation was applied to them because there was nothing to liquidate. The workers were simply fired by -- from work.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: The point of my question was that the word that should be used is emergency measures, but not coercive measures; that's what you tried to say. Extraordinary measures, I'd agree on that, yes. Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: You may call them as you like, but my point is they were implemented through violent measures. Outstanding doctors were taken by police and maltreated, beaten up, and they were -- all of them were Albanians. And I cited here the case of the dean of a faculty of medicine a close collaborator of Mr. Rugova, Dr. Akashi, who was fired from work after having been beaten up and made full of blood all over.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I just wanted to clear up the terminology with you in terms of these extraordinary or emergency measures. Now let's look at paragraph 14. I just wanted to ask you about this paragraph. Do you know at that time Ante Markovic was prime minister of the federal government in Belgrade, the federal government of the SFRY? And that he was carrying out a reform programme. Do you know about that or do you not?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. That will do. Let's move on. Please look at paragraph 36 now. Have a good look. I just have a small question about something that I'm interested in. You said in that paragraph - have you found it? Yes? - that at the end of the talks, you're talking about Rambouillet, all the members of your delegation, the Albanian delegation, wanted to sign the agreement apart from Thaci. Thaci did not want to do that and you explained why it was that he didn't want to do it. That is his own affair, and then you say that ultimately you all signed a letter stating that you would come to Paris and sign this. Is that right, as is written here?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: All right. Now, in the last sentence -- oh, all right. So in Rambouillet you did not sign an agreement, but you signed a pledge stating that you would sign the agreement in Paris. Is that the way it should be interpreted? Or would you explain if this is not correct.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now, I'm just interested in something else in this regard. Let us clarify this fully. In Rambouillet, neither the Serbs, or rather, the Serbian delegation or your delegation did not sign the agreement, right?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And now we're moving on to paragraph 40. We'll move on very quickly if you give short answers. Now you returned to Paris, and as far as I can see, you're saying that there were certain difficulties for you to agree to sign. You say that Dr. Rugova was reluctant; and then you say on the 19th of March, as far as you can remember, you finally signed it. And you say that the Russian ambassador, rather, representative Mayorski - see, it is the last sentence - although still present, refused to sign. Do you still stand by that? What I'm trying to ask you is the following: Do you know why Ambassador Mayorski did not want to sign it?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I may only tell you here that Mr. Mayorski didn't sign the agreement; as to why, you have to ask him.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Right. I just wanted to find out whether perhaps he explained it to you. Now let's look at the next paragraph, paragraph 40. You say that during your stay in Paris, Robin Cook and Hubert Vedrine told you that the bombing would commence soon; then you go on to say in the same paragraph that several members of the Albanian delegation travelled to Brussels and met there Wesley Clark and that he told them that the bombing would start very soon and that you needed to take care of yourselves while the bombing was going on, ensuring that the Albanian population stayed off the streets. Of course, the Serbs could stay on the streets, and then NATO would be there in a few days. Please answer two questions for me: How can they tell you that there would be a bombing when that decision had not been passed yet as far as we know? Because delegations came to Belgrade after that. Are you sure that they said that there would be bombing very soon, in a few days, and that you should only remove Albanians from the streets? Of course, it didn't matter about us. We weren't important.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't present at this meeting, as I have stated here, but it was explained to me what happened. So your question is not a relevant question as to what he said in this case. I can only say that the participants who were there and who met him were told this by him, and that's why I included it in my statement. As to why he asked the question, I can't answer you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And what about Robin Cook? What about Mr. Robin Cook and Mr. Hubert Vedrine, why did they tell you there would be bombing? Truth be told, they didn't tell you to remove Albanians from the streets.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my statement, I simply stated what he said, but I don't know the reason why they said what they said. You have to ask them.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In other words, did they maybe tell you that the decision on bombing had already been passed and that in a few days NATO would be there?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was an international position which was presented initially to the Serbian side, then to the Albanian one.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Very well then. So the Serbs were also told that they would be bombed and that they should stay out of the streets; is that what you're saying? Or are you saying that only you should stay out of the Serbs because only the Serbs would be bombed? Did you hear them say that to the Serb delegation, any of the three men in question? Did you hear it with your own ears? Were you there? Did you witness that?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were, in a way, public statements. These were not rumours said in people's ears. I don't remember whether the Serbs were there or not. That was a publicly knowledge stance; and all the participants knew if they failed to sign the agreement, then the bombing would ensue.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: But you were told that the bombing would take place soon and that NATO would be there in a few days. Where there? What do you mean "there"? How would they be there? How did you understand all that? This is your statement, can you explain?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I may explain by NATO would be there means that a condition imposed by the international community would take effect and failure of the Serbian side to sign the agreement brought NATO in. The pretext to bomb was not encouraged by the Albanians but by the Serbs with their failing to sign the agreement, and there are official documents to prove that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: This is not what I asked you. I'm not asking you this. I'm asking you how you understood the statement that NATO would be there in a few days. What was that? What were you saying when you said that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, don't you think that's been answered clearly?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think so because we're talking about NATO, not the international community. We've had numerous witnesses who testified to the fact that NATO wouldn't be there. That's why I'm asking the question. You had Panic and others amongst others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's why I'm putting that question, but let's move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The witness has just told you: "I may explain by NATO would be there means a position imposed would take effect and failure of the Serbian side to sign the agreement brought NATO in. The pretext to bomb was not encouraged by the Albanians but by the Serbs with their failing to sign." So it clearly says that that means that NATO would start bombing.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In paragraphs from 50 to 52, you're talking about the conditions of life of Dr. Rugova. You went there and you termed that as house prison, house arrest. As far as I understand, you moved through Pristina in your car until the moment you moved in with Dr. Rugova; and even later on you moved around by car. You would leave the house. You would come back to the house. Did I understand all that well? And you reported to Dr. Rugova what you saw around Pristina, what was happening. Is that correct, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could leave the house escorted by the police, because I wanted to see the city and to inform the media outlets of what was happening in Pristina. That was the first reason. Mr. Rugova never went out to visit Pristina, and we were under house arrest and I can prove this by giving you two facts because this is what you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Please answer my questions. Did you have telephone contacts with whomever you wanted, including even Mr. Hill in Skopje? You told us yesterday that you spoke to him on the phone? Did you have mobile phones that you could use to communicate? Can you please answer by saying yes or no, please.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't have a mobile phone but I had a fixed telephone.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... You had contacts with journalists, foreign journalists, and everybody else?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did have some communications by phone, but it was sometimes cut off, depending on various tactics used. I used a telephone when it was working to inform the world that we were alive, because that was argument for us to save our lives.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Very well. You will agree with me that if they had wanted to kill you, they would have done that because you had 20 armed persons in the house. You could not have saved your life over telephone; wouldn't you agree with that? What I'm interested in is the fact that you had the possibility to communicate with the external world, and at one point you sent your family could you tell to Skopje. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, there was a question. Does he want an answer to the question or are we moving on to something else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now we have two questions. I object. Could we have one at a time, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, one at a time.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you send your family to Skopje, this is my question, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: My family went to Skopje by itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I'm saying. And at one point you went to Skopje yourself and then returned after that; correct?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. You can find it in my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I'm not disputing anything that you stated. I'm just asking you questions. And now I'm interested in something else. You say in paragraph 59 that you wrote a letter to Milosevic. My question to you is this: Do you happen to have a copy of that letter? We would like to see what it says in that letter. To jog your memory, please look at paragraph 59. Don't you have it?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't have that letter with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I would really be curious to see what it says in that letter. And now I'll move really fast because there's nothing disputable about what I'm going to ask you. There has been a lot of confusion about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before you move on. Are you saying you do have a copy somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I prepared that letter on the spot and gave it to the first policeman to convey to the person, because that was the first possibility I had to communicate. That was -- that contained a demand that we had to leave Kosova. I want to have it in writing to prove that we had requested to leave Kosova.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Before we move on, can you please agree with me or not - and the question is following - that in 1999 there was a SR Yugoslavia, which was a state of Serbia and Montenegro. It had a federal government and a federal prime minister. Would you agree with that or not?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: There was also the president of the Republic of Serbia, the president of Montenegro. There is the president of the federal state. There was the prime minister and the Government of the Serbia as well as of Montenegro, and there was also the president and the prime minister of the federal government. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. But as I said, these institutions were not recognised by the Albanians of Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I'm not asking you this question because of that. Very well. But this is not my point. We've established that the president of Yugoslavia was Milosevic. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: The president of Serbia was Milan Milutinovic?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I regret, Your Honour, to say this, but I am here. If I can say this, if I can say these are very ordinary questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, can we get to the point, please? We know all these basic facts. As soon as you -- you start asking him, the witness starts wondering what's going on and hesitates to answer. Just get to the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the essence of my objection to Mr. Hannis's questions which was refuted, but now I will clarify.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: The president of the federal government, the prime minister, was Momir Bulatovic, would you agree with that? Do you know that? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And Nikola Sainovic was one of the vice-presidents of the federal government. Wouldn't that be correct? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know accurately what his position was, but probably that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Very well. Do you know anything about the ranking of the political officials? Who is more important, the president of the republic, the prime minister, or a vice-president in the government? In your view, which one of them is the most important?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And now let's go to Kosovo. The first time you saw Sainovic was on the 4th of April, 1999. On the 5th of April, did you see him at all or not? Just to be clear on that. We had some confusion about the dates, and I'm talking about paragraph 62 where the dates were corrected. If you can remember, of course. Paragraph 62.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first time we met was on the 4th; while on the 6th, we met again on the occasion of the Russian Ambassador Kotov's visit.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And the 5th --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a second. In paragraph 64, you say that you met on the 5th, and you're talking about the Russian ambassador's visit in paragraph 63. So it may not be vitally important, but do you remember whether it was the 5th or the 6th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 4th, we met for the first time. He came with a request for us to meet Markovic. On the next day, the Russian ambassador came for a visit, and Mr. Sainovic attended this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... On the 5th?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my recollection, yes, it's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And now you saw him on TV once. You mentioned a Crisis Staff, and this is also in paragraph 64, if I understand you well?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw him sitting around this table, and I mentioned this very short, several-seconds-long clip.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: The question is this: Was this only once?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only once, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Very well. Again, we are facing a dilemma. He told you something about not being able to guarantee your safety if you moved abroad. What I'm not clear about is whether you were to go abroad on your own or with Mr. Rugova. Who was supposed to go abroad? Can you explain that? I don't have any objections to your answer. I just didn't understand. I'm seeking clarification.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: My explanation is this, and it will be the 50th after I've come here to testify. Our request was always for them to allow myself, Mr. Rugova, and all of us who were there to leave. This was our categorical request.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I didn't ask you that. We agree on that. I don't have any objections. I did not understand you. The warning, "I cannot guarantee your safety." The words uttered to you by Sainovic, did it apply to your travel to Skopje or to you travelling together, the two of you? I know that you sought to go abroad, but I'm not sure about this security and safety remark. What did that apply to? Do you understand my question? Only that, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was clear. We discussed the request to leave; and when we discussed my leaving, it is correct that he said that there will be security concerns.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And he's talking about you personally.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: This is what I wanted, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The answer was yes, and it should be recorded and it hasn't been. Mr. Merovci's answer was yes to the question about his personal safety. Line 33.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Could you please repeat --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, there's no magic wand that line 33. The fact that you've stated the position and no one has dissented is all that will going to happen at this stage, so move on please. You're not going to alter it at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay, let's move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The one thing you can do is ask the witness to clarify it. It's the way you ask the questions that makes it difficult for him. If you would ask him the simple question, who was Sainovic referring to when he said you're free to go but we cannot guarantee your security, you might get a simple answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But he did answer that, he meant him personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Isn't that correct, Mr. Merovci?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: That's that. And now let's move on to paragraph -- just a moment, please, 68. In paragraph 73, actually, yesterday you mentioned for the first time that you met with Mr. Slobodan Milosevic. Somebody asked you that, and you said that Milosevic told you that you could go with your family, if I understood you well. I would like to clarify this. In paragraph 73, if you look at your statement, nothing is being said about Milosevic and you said it yesterday. What would be your final statement? Who was it who told you and Mr. Rugova that you and Mr. Rugova could leave with your families? Was it Mr. Milosevic? That's my question.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And just one more thing. In paragraph 68, you say that you had several talks with Mr. Sainovic and that you warned him in one of those talks - and it really doesn't matter what paragraph it is - and a mention is made of Racak, and then he said that Walter [as interpreted] is making things up. Did I understand you well that a reference is made to Racak in that statement of yours? Did I understand you well?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And something else I would like to know. On several occasions, Sainovic turned up at your place once he proposed a meeting with Ratko Markovic, who was the president of the delegation. The second time he told you that you should meet with Milutinovic. The Prosecutor asked you why Markovic but he didn't ask you why Milutinovic because it didn't suit him, but I'm asking you now. Was Sainovic the spokesman who was sent to make proposals or he was a decision-maker? Was he just an envoy who was bringing messages or was he a decision-maker who told you what you should do? On one occasion, he spoke about Markovic, on another occasion Milutinovic? What was his role? This is what I'm interested in. If you have a problem with that, let me explain.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my opinion - and you're looking for my opinion- what his role was, what his function was, you can ask him. But I think you're looking here for my personal opinion, and to my understanding Mr. Sainovic was the person who came more frequently and announced meetings. In a way, he could have been the person who acted in a capacity of an envoy, who conveyed opinions of higher ranks.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila. Mr. Fila --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, this is all --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What paragraph is the reference to encouraging him to meet Markovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In paragraph 62, Markovic; and Milutinovic is mentioned in 67.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And you started or part of that question says: "But the Prosecutor didn't ask you why Milutinovic because it didn't suit him, but I'm asking you now," and then you diverted attention away from that. Are you asking that question? It certainly hasn't been answered?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, do you want to ask it?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. I just wanted to add that question because Prosecutor only deemed that Ratko Markovic was important, and I'm wondering why he didn't mention Milutinovic and a message from Milutinovic. But now I understand. I'm clear on that and I don't have any more questions. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Visnjic. Shall we break now and start slightly earlier and have you a clear -- do you have questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions, and I can finish even before the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. That's clear. Mr. Aleksic, you do have questions, do you?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one. Thank you, Your Honour, just one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One brief question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Merovci. Just one question with regard to your conversation with my colleague Fila, and paragraph 41 you were at the meeting. What Mr. Cook and Mr. Vedrine told you, you say that several members of the delegation went to Brussels. Can you tell us, if you know, which members of your delegation travelled to Brussels to meet with Wesley Clark? Which members of the delegation were those?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the Albanian delegation, several went. I don't remember exactly how many, five or six maybe. Among them was Mrs. Edita Tahiri, who conveyed this information to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Among these five or six members, were there any members of the KLA who went to Brussels?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That will be all. I don't have any further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Cepic, you do have questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do have questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll break now. As before, Mr. Merovci, we have to break for 20 minutes or so, so could you leave the courtroom with the usher and we'll resume at 10 minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Merovci. I'm Djuro Cepic, one of the Defence attorneys on the Defence teams. I have several questions to you. I'll do my best to put clear, concrete questions, and please respond as briefly as possible so that we could move through this as fast as possible. Mr. Merovci, I'm just going to deal with a topic that my learned friend Mr. Milutinovic questioned you about, that is to say trade in immovable property. Just one question: Do you know that these provisions were in force throughout the territory of Serbia. Like in Kosovo, it was also valid in Sumadija, in Serbia proper, in Vojvodina, and throughout? Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my knowledge, it referred to Kosova only; because if these measures were to provide Serbs from selling their property, it is logical that they were limited to Kosova only.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: So that's your assumption, right? It is not an assertion on the basis of the actual article from that law.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, he answered that was "to my knowledge." I think he has limited it that way already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think the question is legitimate, Mr. Hannis. Can you explain whether it's -- that's your assumption or whether you actually have read the law?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've not read the law, Your Honour, but I'm speaking of what was going on in reality. If we refer to what Mr. Fila said just before, that this law was in force in order to prevent the Serbs from moving out from Kosova, it is logical for me to conclude that this law was referred to Kosova only. This was what I wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Merovci, let us go back to your statement, as well as to what you said yesterday during your direct examination conducted by Mr. Hannis in this same courtroom. On page 18 of yesterday's transcript, and in paragraph 31 of your statement, you say that you were aware of the Milosevic-Holbrooke Agreement. And after it was signed in October 1998, you were with Dr. Rugova and Mr. Christopher Hill in a vehicle in Kosovo on the road between Stimlje and Suva Reka. Where -- thank you. Where did you see the soldiers of the Army of Yugoslavia? Yesterday you said that there were tanks there and APCs as well. My question is whether you are fully aware of the Milosevic-Holbrooke Agreement, in its entirety, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object. There are two questions. Is he asking him about the tanks or is he asking him about the Holbrooke agreement?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I read the question as first of all dealing the issue with whether the witness is fully aware --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, I apologise. I think there is a problem in translation, because I said on which road you saw VJ soldiers not the question: Where did you see the soldiers. This is line -- this is line 39, line 1-- page 39, line 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It still contains the possibility of two questions, Mr. Cepic. But the first question that needs to be answered, Mr. Merovci, is whether you're fully aware of terms of the Milosevic-Holbrooke Agreement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I didn't see this agreement in a written form. The information I got was from what was communicated through the media.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic will now follow-up on that. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And do you know perhaps that perhaps by this very same agreement, that is to say the Holbrooke-Milosevic Agreement, what was precisely spelled out was that a certain number of units of the Army of Yugoslavia should be in the area, in the field, in order to protect certain roads, inter alia precisely this particular road: Stimlje-Suva Reka. And those units were at that location and at that time precisely in accordance with the provisions of that agreement?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I already said, I did not read this agreement. I did not see it in a written form.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Merovci. We'll move on to paragraph 39 of your statement in which you describe the period between two rounds of negotiations in Rambouillet; and you say that in that period in Kosovo, the atmosphere in Kosovo was very strange that could be described as a lull before the storm. Do you know that in that period, that is to say during the negotiations in Rambouillet, the forces of the so-called KLA considerably intensified their actions and attacks, both against civilians and members of the army and the police, which was indeed established by the Kosovo Verification Mission?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Merovci. Do you perhaps know how big a territory was held by the so-called KLA at the moment when the Holbrooke-Milosevic Agreement was signed, and how big a territory they held on the eve of the bombing, approximately?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: And do you know, perhaps, that it was precisely due to terrorist actions taken by the so-called KLA during the first 80 days of 1999 over 100 civilians were killed, several policemen and soldiers, some were even kidnapped. Do you know anything about that, Mr. Merovci?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your question is prejudiced. The terms you are using are unacceptable for me, and my answer is no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What part of the question do you find unacceptable?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When the counsel says that the KLA actions were terrorist ones, they don't go together in my opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic, it's a matter for you, but if we really want to get to the heart of the issues in the case, it's not helpful to constantly refer to the KLA as the so-called KLA because that's you speaking not so much as counsel, but from a sort of Serb standpoint which I don't think is the right way to deal with it. I entirely excuse the use of the word "terrorist," but again -- and I can understand that. I expect I've used the expression myself at some stage in the trial. But bearing in mind what happens when this sort of language is used, then it's better I think to be more sensitive. Now, do you want to rephrase that question and confine it to KLA activity, which then removes the objection that the witness finds to the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I understood. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Merovci, even if I were not to use the word "terrorist," your answer would remain the same, right?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I would like to know your knowledge of this, Mr. Merovci. The question was: Were you aware that during the first 80 days of 1999, the KLA were responsible for the deaths of more than a hundred civilians and several policemen and soldiers, and they were also responsible for some kidnappings. Now, do you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can only say that it is possible that I heard this information, but for the Albanian side this information was irrelevant because it came from the side that committed massacres and killings in Kosova. This data for the Albanian side was irrelevant. If I say "yes," then it will confirm this. That's why my answer is that I don't know about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you see, we're not in Kosovo just now, and we're not fighting the battle of 1999 at the moment. We're trying to take an impartial view of the circumstances, and it would be helpful to us if you could try to lay aside your natural reluctance to say anything that might be interpreted as somehow or other favouring a Serb point of view and tell us whether as a matter of fact you as I think so far, certainly following Mr. O'Sullivan's line, you as the group trying to approach this from the peaceful point of view were, in fact, aware that there was another group of people who were killing civilians. Now, are you saying you were unaware of that or are you saying it's just that you can't confirm the exact figures or what is your position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this clarifies the question. If the counsel asks questions with figures, with hundreds, then my answer is that I don't know the figures, the exact figures; however, I did hear information about this, but I also know that the KLA platform comprised of the fight against the forces that were considered aggressor in Kosova.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, can I make it really simple and ask you if you were aware that the KLA were responsible for killing some civilians in the early part of 1999.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I'm not aware of this, that the KLA killed civilians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Merovci, you should know that at the end of 1998 the KLA kidnapped several activists of the party that you belonged to, the LDK.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This I know. But the way it was interpreted by these people themselves, they even released a press statement. These people said that they were not kidnapped, that they had an interview with certain KLA members. These statements can be found at a press conference that was organised in relation to this case you are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Merovci. Yesterday on transcript page 24, lines 8 and 10, you said that before the bombing started a few shops owned by Albanians were destroyed. The specific number you gave was four or five shops. My question is whether the Cafe Koka and Cafe Medji were among these shops. These cafes were destroyed on the 22nd of March, 1999, in Pristina of course.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly because the names you mentioned do not ring a bell. I don't know which these cafes are. I used as an illustration a private clinic called Rezonanca situated in Dardania neighbourhood. It was a solid, concrete building. Explosives were laid and the entire building was blown up.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Merovci. I put a specific question, so please give shorter answers so that we will move on as fast as possible. Are you aware at all of attacks perpetrated by persons unknown and that were later accepted by the KLA as being their own in terms of throwing explosive devices into cafes, shops, and other facilities in Pristina, not to mention all of them specifically and not to waste any time. There were several such incidents and there were several casualties involved. Do you know anything about that, Mr. Merovci?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my knowledge, this is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: What would you say to me if I were to say to you that all of these incidents were verified by the Kosovo Verification Mission?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a leading question, a prejudiced question. I would give you the same answer. I don't know and I don't think that is the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Merovci. Yesterday, during your testimony in relation to the direct questions put to you by the learned Prosecutor, you said that between your Tuesdays in France, in accordance with the information you received from the Kosovo Information Centre and information was provided by activists of the party you belonged to, that the presence of Serb troops increased by 30.000 at that. What would you say to me if I were to say to you that no one ever referred to this particular bit of information, either the Kosovo Verification Mission or any other source for that matter; even you in your previous statements and in your testimony in the Milosevic trial never referred to that. You first mentioned it yesterday.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will give you the same explanation as yesterday. This is about the period between the Rambouillet and Paris conference when the verification missions could no longer perform their tasks, and this is verified by the fact that they left thereafter. This number is an approximate number. It continued to increase later on. This information was collected by our activists in the field. It is an approximate figure; and, as I already said, this number increased and it is within the estimate given by international institutions as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mr. Merovci, I looked at all the reports of the Kosovo Verification Mission and I did my best and I made an enormous effort to look into other documents as well and nowhere did I find the figures that you referred to yesterday. Your Honour, or rather His Honour, the Presiding Judge, yesterday put a question on page 20 in relation to that, whether there was any material available from the Kosovo Verification Mission that would corroborate such an assertion. You stand by what you claimed yesterday, right? Or would you agree with me that you were not quite well-informed?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now you're trying to paraphrase my answer. I never said that the verification mission gave this figure. This figure is a result of the activity of our activists in the field. During this time when we were able to collect information, this figure came up; however, later assessments speak of an increased presence later on. This is what I'm trying to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Merovci. Yesterday, while making a statement, you said that most information on the arrival of Serb troops was received from your activists in the area of Podujevo, where your activists say they were following the movement of troops. Do you know that most of that territory, that is to say of the municipality of Podujevo, was under KLA control?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
