utterances.text: Your Honour, can we have a date related to that question, because Mr. Merovci is talking particularly about the date between Rambouillet and Paris.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I specified the period between two conferences in the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So we can assume that this question also deals with that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My answer is this: The Merdare-Prishtine road was free from movement, and your claim doesn't hold water when you say that you could not use this road because of the KLA presence.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Do you know that on that very road that you've just mentioned, there were frequent attacks on the members of the army, police, as well as on civilians?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that the KLA was active in this area, based on the information at the time, but I do not know of any attack of the KLA on civilians, except for attacks on police and army.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: You personally never went there. You were never present there were you?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would like us to talk about the negotiations. Both my colleagues Fila and Aleksic asked you about the announcement of bombing, the information that you heard from Mr. Cook and Mr. Vedrine before you left Paris. Did you personally provide that information to the journalists? Did you tell them that bombing would start soon, or was it somebody else from your delegation who did that?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was not a secret piece of information; it was public knowledge. The journalists were there all the time, and the issue of bombing was a transparent condition imposed by the international community to be used in case of the failure of the Rambouillet agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Upon your return to Kosovo, the plane landed in Tirana where members of the KLA descended; then you and Mr. Rugova got into a car across the border-crossing in Djeneral Jankovic. You went towards Pristina, and coming towards you were vehicles, a lot of vehicles, carrying civilians and representatives of international community. Would you please tell me what date was that. Was it the 20th or the 21st of March, 1999?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This happened on the 21st of March, and that happened in Hani i Elezet, not Hani i Hotit, and we drove to Skopje by car. And we flew from Tirana to Skopje; and from Skopje to Pristina, we drove and crossed the border at Hani i Elezet. It's is a border-crossing with Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Do you maybe know that long columns of civilians in civilian cars were on the road headed towards Montenegro and Merdare, in the hinterland of Serbia. Are you aware of that, Mr. Merovci?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you are talking about that day, that day I was at the border-crossing point of Hani i Elezet, and I can testify to what I saw there. What you are putting to me happened in other places, in other roads, which I couldn't see.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us now look at 31st of March, 1999. In your statement - and yesterday on direct - you stated that in the neighbourhood where Dr. Rugova's house was, members of the MUP - and among them there were even some soldiers who were armed - had previously expelled people from some houses, and then they broke through the gate of the house where you were together with Dr. Rugova's family. You described them as some of them wearing the uniforms of the former Yugoslav army and the others wore either black or dark blue uniforms. On these uniforms, you did not see the inscription of the Army of Yugoslavia, did you, Mr. Merovci?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've seen the emblems and the people were there, but I want to make a correction. In your question you make assumptions which are not correct. Even though you are not asking me, I want to correct it because otherwise it would be implied as if I accept that. It's not a question of several houses and people, but it's a matter for the entire neighbourhood, the cleansing of the entire neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: We understand that from your statement. I'm now asking you about the insignia and inscriptions. On the insignia, you did not see the inscription of the Army of Yugoslavia, did you, Mr. Merovci?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I saw them. The uniform was that of the Yugoslav army.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: My question was very clear and it was about the insignia and inscriptions. Did you see the words the "Army of Yugoslavia" on the insignia? This is what I asked you. I didn't ask you about the uniforms.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw only two letters, V and J.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: What if I were to tell you that in the Army of Yugoslavia does not know of any such abbreviation on the insignia? There is no abbreviation have the "VJ" on any of the Army of Yugoslavia insignia.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is your question now? You have no question for me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm not clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The question you're being asked is: Knowing, or being told that by counsel representing a senior army figure, being told that there is no such -- or was at that time no such insignia with simply the letters V and J, do you still say that you saw insignia with these letters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I'm clear about the question. The counsel is saying: What if I tell you that there were no such letters? And my answer to that question is: The Yugoslav uniform, because I'm going to speak about something which occurred eight years ago, that uniform was very familiar to us. We saw them, the soldiers, wearing them every day on the streets and they were equipped with various kinds of armaments. Now it appears that there was no letter -- that there were no letters V and J. If that were the case, that -- still, that does not refute what I said, that they were Yugoslav forces. I know that the question is whether I've seen these things or not; but very sincerely, I can tell you that maybe it was not exactly V and J. But most probably the letters were the ones that I mentioned, because we were in very difficult situations to concentrate and look properly at such details. But as far as I know, this was uniform of the Yugoslav army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Merovci. Let's move on. Further on in your statement you say that Mr. Jankovic, a major, appeared in a blue police uniform; and in your view, he was in command of the unit that was housed in that house. This is your claim, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a person that was a person with whom I had the first communication after having been detained or kept in a hole for four hours, all of us together. He was the first man to communicate with us, and he was dressed in a police uniform with rankings on his shoulders and he introduced himself to me saying --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Merovci. Yesterday you said that you believed that he was in command of the unit; that was on page 33 of yesterday's transcript. Further on, on page 37, lines 3 and 4, you say that later on Mr. Joksic appeared from the state security and that you realised that he was in charge, that Joksic was in charge and that Jankovic was in command of that unit. Mr. Merovci, what would you tell me if I were to tell you that in keeping with the law and the rules of the then-Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, Republic of Serbia, and the laws of other armed forces in other states, a police officer cannot be in command of a military unit or any of the troops thereof?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is your assumption. Now I have a question for you. What is your question for me?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mr. Merovci, I'm the one asking questions here. I'm trying to be as clear and as specific possible, and I'm imploring you to give me short and precise answers and I thank you in advance. I have provided you with the basis for my question, having told you that in keeping with the laws and regulations in the then-Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, the Republic of Serbia, as well as in many other countries across the world, there is no such an example in which a police officer would be in command of an entire military unit or part thereof, nowhere. And I'm providing you with the legal basis for that, and I am asking you to answer my question for the second time, please. And the question is the same as before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, what is --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Am I right in saying this --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What is the question, Mr. Cepic? I mean, it's a speech you're making that the law is clear, a policeman can't command the army. What we're dealing with here is a witness who's telling us what he experienced on the ground, so there's little point in asking him about political or military theory.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if you will allow me, I just wanted to clarify certain things, and I wanted to compare the things that the witness has provided with so far with the actual facts. But I believe that the answer to my previous question has provided us with a clear view that he had of the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, I think you should move on, Mr. Cepic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mr. Merovci, yesterday, on page 25 of the LiveNote, you stated that there were paramilitaries in Pristina and that they created panic among the population, and then you said something that you never said before throughout the seven years, either in any of your statements or in the Milosevic case; and that is that after the panic was created by the paramilitary formations, the police, and the military would simply move people out. Did somebody instruct you to testify in that way, the way you testified yesterday? Did somebody suggest that you should say something that you had not say for the past seven years?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Merovci. Yesterday, on your direct, you talked about the killing of Mr. Kelmendi and his two sons. This was recorded on page 25 of yesterday's transcript. You spoke with Mrs. Kelmendi on the 26th of March, 1999, in Pristina, immediately after this tragic event. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: She told you what had happened. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: How come that if you had the information on the 26th of March, 1999, until yesterday you claimed that this was done by members of the paramilitary formations, and then yesterday you decided to change that statement of yours? Am I right in saying that your memory was much fresher, much more accurate immediately after the event?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you repeat the question. I'm not clear about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: You will agree with me, Mr. Merovci, will you not, that your memory was much fresher in the course of 1999 and 2000, closer to the event itself?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. What you are saying is not true. It's not a question of memory we are talking about here; it's a question of information. At the time I visited Mrs. Kelmendi, in a very pathetic way, she explained what happened. And for your information, Your Honours, the military and the police forces for the bulk of the Albanian population were one and the same in the way they perceived them, because they did what they did in unison. And the narration of Mrs. Kelmendi was exactly as I have stated in my 2000 statement. Therefore, as I'm saying, it's not a question of memory. It's a question of further information I found out, and we learned that they were military forces. So in my statement the sentence starts with "paramilitaries." But when it comes to Mr. Kelmendi, it's not implied that they were paramilitaries. If you read that statement carefully, you will see that I did not explicitly mean these forces in the case of Kelmendi. Maybe if you read it differently, you may understand it differently, as the counsel put it to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mr. Merovci, I've read your statement carefully several times. I've studied everything you have stated very carefully, and yesterday the Presiding Judge asked you about the differences in your statements on two or three occasions. Just briefly, after such a long period of time, after seven years, your statement yesterday differed from what you stated in your statement given in 2000 and particularly in reference to the killing of Mr. Kelmendi and his sons, the 30.000 Serbs that were brought to Kosovo, the persecution that was done by the military, the police, and the paramilitaries in Pristina. You mentioned a journalist who was present in Rugova's house, and you did that only yesterday, never before that. And some other differences. All that I have mentioned just now you did not mention, either in your statements or in the Milosevic case. You only mentioned all those things yesterday. Likewise, yesterday, the Presiding Judge asked you about --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I find it very difficult to find what question that the witness can answer you are about to pose after that speech. Let's concentrate on questioning the witness, not summarising your closing arguments.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I've been trying to do it as quickly as I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But combining all these allegations together isn't going to get us an answer that's going to take you anywhere, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I agree with you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mr. Merovci, I have mentioned a number of discrepancies that exist between your statement, the transcript, and the testimony provided in the courtroom yesterday and today. Did somebody maybe suggest what you should state today in this courtroom? Did maybe somebody instruct you what to say?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I object to the form of the question. Discrepancies, he needs to point out some specific things. If he's talking about the things he listed in the speech before, a number of them aren't discrepancies. They're things he didn't mention before. They are additions. A couple of them were in the supplemental information which we provided before we came in. So it wasn't just yesterday he told us about them. He told us about a couple of those things the day before. We put it in his supplemental information we gave before he came here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think the first thing you have to do, Mr. Cepic, is specify a discrepancy, which I would understand to be a contradiction between what was said in evidence yesterday and what the said in the statement on a previous occasion. Now, can we identify a discrepancy and then you can ask him a question specifically in relation to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if you allow me to say, I already asked all those questions about Mr. Kelmendi, about the Serbian troops, about extermination in Pristina. I already --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Hold on again. The 30.000 troops isn't a discrepancy. That's putting a firm figure on a vague statement that existed before, and then making it clear that in it in itself is only an estimate based on information coming in from a wide range of sources. On the other hand, the question of paramilitaries and being involved in the killing of Kelmendi or VJ forces being involved is potentially a discrepancy, but the witness explained already that the impression people in Pristina had was that the army and the police acted as one. They were one and the same thing, and it was only later when he got more information about it that he realised that Mrs. Kelmendi was lumping everybody together and that in fact there was more specific information. So in fact you've got an explanation for that. Now, what you're -- what you want to ask here is whether somebody has influenced the evidence of the witness, and your basis for that is saying that, first of all, there's more meat on the skeleton of his original statement; and, secondly, that in some instances it might be suggested there's a change in his evidence. Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Exactly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Merovci, has been influencing what you have to say here? That's what Mr. Cepic wants to know. Because information is coming out, either differently from the way in which it appears in your original statement or with more added on. Now, what do you have to say to that question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, even in earlier question asked of me whether someone has influenced -- has asked me to speak differently, I gave the answer. With respect to my statement of 2000 ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please carry on, Mr. Merovci.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My testimony given in 2002 and my coming here in 2007 from this -- from the time that has passed, what I'm saying now doesn't run counter to what I said before; otherwise, why am I here?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, if you want to follow-up on this, Mr. Cepic, you should take one example and deal with it exclusively, because as soon as you lump two together you run into difficulties, either of interpreting whether there is a difference or simply an additional piece of information. So if you want to follow this up in any detail, you'll have to take one example and put a specific point to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I will continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Merovci, speaking about the killings, do you know approximately when Mr. Xhemail Mustafa was killed, and he was a close associate of Dr. Rugova?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was killed sometime after 2000. I am not sure about the accurate date.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Was the perpetrator ever discovered? Is it known who killed him?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until now, no, no public information has been released to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: And what about Mr. Ismet Raci, a high official of the SK and a president of the municipality of Klina who was buried in 2001 when he was killed? Was the perpetrator of that killing ever discovered?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I fail to see the relevance of killings in 2000 and 2001.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: About relation in Kosovo between -- between political party LDK and others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And what's the relevance to the indictment of the relationship in 2000?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I will change the topic, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: That was the last question in that area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Just about the relations in Kosovo it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Merovci, and now something about you personally. You were the general manager of the postal services and the telecom of Kosovo. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at Defence Exhibit 5D81.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have an objection about the relevance of this. I'm not sure when he had this job and the document I see I have one page of a story about something. I don't see the relevance of it. If we can have some --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it's a matter that definitely arises out of evidence in chief, because you led evidence from the witness that that's what his job had been. And until I hear another question on the subject, it's impossible to say whether it's out of order or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Merovci, am I right if I say that in 2002, in October, you were suspended from that position due to certain suspicions expressed with regard to you personally?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was -- I got that position as a result of a public announcement and I was in that position for ten months, but my work there was concentrated on fighting corruption and misuses of powers. And because of my public announcements of misuses carried out in that institution, I was suspended from my work because of breaching the rules of public communication. Quite unlawfully I was suspended from my work, and I was not expelled from my position. I was simply suspended, and that was the case until the expiry of my contract, which was not renewed. The reason for my suspension, as I said once, was publishing of misuses in the course of the work committed by senior officials. And for that, there are documents, public documents, and the entire public in Kosova is familiar with that. You can have access to that page and see for yourselves all this information.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: So after this suspension you were no longer director of the post office and the telecom, right?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: After my suspension, I remained director of post service. You should know the meaning of the word "suspension." It's not expulsion. It's just a specific status given to someone until his case is examined and a decision has been made. But as I said, there were three more months before my contract expired, and they refused to consider my case, and this is why I'm saying it is unlawful. Because if someone is suspended, you have to take a measure either to punish him, impose a fine, or to fire him. In my case, nothing was done. They just waited until my contract expired, and this went on for three months and it was not renewed. And I took legal proceedings against the management, and the case is in the second-degree court.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Merovci. In the Albanian media, primarily in the Koha Ditore newspaper, an article was published by the UNMIK office for public information in Kosovo; and it says, precisely in this article that it refers to your suspension which is 5D81, that you were Mr. Rugova's personal body-guard. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already explained this yesterday. My official title as to what function I performed, there wasn't any. Nobody had that. My job was to look after the office of Mr. Rugova. I covered two fields: The field of his security and his protocol. For your knowledge, security and protocol are closely linked fields. Those who write and comment these things in different articles, it is their problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Merovci. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: No further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, before we go to the next, he mentioned Exhibit 5D81. I don't know if he proposes to put that in. If he does, what I've been provided with is only one page of a story. Either we should have the whole story in or not at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't think we want it, Mr. Hannis. Mr. Cepic made from it the point that he wanted to make that there was a statement of the position of the witness; that purpose having been achieved, there's no purpose in admitting this document, I think. I'm concerned about the nature of the document, Mr. Cepic. We've been quite firm so far that newspaper reports are generally forms of evidence we are not anxious to proceed upon. I accept that generally we allow the documents in to the extent they've been used for the purpose of questions, but in this case I don't think we should have this -- a document of this nature when it was adequate for you to quote from it to put your question. If, later, there's some reason for you to try to introduce this as part of your case, then the position may be different.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, just one sentence, by your leave. Precisely due to the fact that this was published by the UN Mission in Kosovo that selects newspaper articles, the -- it was their Department of Public Information that dealt with this, and that is why I tendered this article. It's not a mere news article. It went through the selection process of the UN mission in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That doesn't, I'm afraid, change the nature of the document. This is just their selection of what they consider to be newsworthy items. This is just journalism, and journalism is not, generally speaking, evidence for our purposes. So in this exceptional situation, we will not admit the document, even for the purpose of putting everything in context because that purpose has been adequately served by the quotation from the document. And as I said already, that doesn't stop you trying to introduce it on some legitimate basis at a later stage if you think that could possibly be acceptable evidence for us. All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. But I would like to ask for something else, to have something admitted into evidence, and I hope that you will agree to that. The transcripts of Mr. Merovci's testimony in the case against Mr. Milosevic; 5D77, that is, and 5D80. So could that please be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, is that his entire transcript for both days when he testified?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sounds like it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Both days.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I have no objection, Your Honour. We were satisfied to present his statement, but I have no objection to you receiving his testimony as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic, we are not opposed in principle to the idea of admitting testimony from the Milosevic trial. Is it not possible, however, to be more selective than simply put everything in, or have you a particular reason why everything should be tendered?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that we did specify two pages that I would like to have admitted as special exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Oh, sorry. We thought it was the entire transcript for two days, but you're saying it's only two pages? That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, knowing that my learned friend Mr. Hannis will object to my proposal and wishing to safe-guard my interests, I proposed both days, but it would be much simpler for the sake of the evidence and for the sake of this Defence if you were to admit two separate pages that we have already prepared as special exhibits. So I would just kindly like to ask for a bit of time while Mr. Lukic is putting his questions, we are going to say exactly which pages they are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's fine, but were we right in understanding that 5D77 is the transcript for one day and 5D80 is the transcript for the other day?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, precisely. 5D77 is the 24th of May, and 5D80 is the 23rd of May, 2002.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you can clarify the position later before we conclude today's business. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Merovci. I'm Branko Lukic, and I will have some questions for you today. I would just briefly like to go back to what you discussed with Mr. Cepic today on page 44, line 17. Mr. Cepic asked you about the reporting of the Kosovo Verification Mission, about KLA attacks. You said that you think that that is not correct, so I'd like to ask you the following. Do you have any knowledge about the Kosovo Verification Mission providing erroneous information about what happened in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I have no knowledge about any erroneous information.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What are your grounds, then, for not accepting what Mr. Cepic put to you in relation to KLA attacks referred to in the reports of the Kosovo Verification Mission?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I think he answered that question that he didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely. Then I'm trying to get an answer from the witness as to the grounds on which he does not accept what had been put to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it's not as clear as that, Mr. Lukic. The witness was being asked whether he knew that there had been -- that the KLA were responsible for the deaths that were referred to, and I certainly wouldn't read that as, Had you read about it in KVM reports? Or, Now that we tell you the KVM say so, do you know? The witness is quite simply saying he doesn't know about that. He's not says, I doubt the report from another source. So I think your question starts off on the wrong basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I can move on, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I would like to go back to page 46, again something that my colleague Mr. Cepic asked you about, and we're talking about the Merdare-Pristina road. In your testimony, you stated that your activists had stated that between two conferences, the Rambouillet conference and the Paris conference, that is, about 30.000 Serb troops entered the area. You also told us that you know that the KLA was active in the area of Podujevo; and in response to Mr. Cepic's question, you said that you did not know about KLA attacks against civilians in the area. Is it your testimony today that your activists never reported about these KLA attacks against civilians from the area in which, in your view, they were informed about the entry of Serb troops in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no relevant sources about things you're saying, that what if a certain KLA committed attacks on civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I asked you whether your activists ever reported about these attacks, or is it your assertion today that they never reported about such attacks?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did not report.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now I would like to focus on paragraph 4 of your statement when you say that in 1981 patrols were introduced. There were always three officers on these patrols, one being Albanian and two others Serbs. Mr. Merovci, is it actually correct that the patrols would consist of one Albanian and two non-Albanians; meaning a Croat, a Slovene, a Hungarian, a Muslim? It wasn't compulsory to one have one Albanian and two Serbs?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: To us it was an Albanian and two non-Albanian. I'm not denying that these other two could have been members of other communities.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. In paragraph 5, you refer to Slobodan Milosevic's sentence when he addressed the Serbs that were assembled and he said something to the effect of, "No one will dare to beat you again," in 1987 that is. Who were the Serbs -- who was it that beat the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The translation was wrong. I didn't ask who were the Serbs but who beat the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was a spectacular political visit that he paid in order to be able to continue with his policy against Albanians. I don't know who he referred to when he said, "Nobody would beat you again." This was a speech that was broadcast on television, and I interpreted it the way I heard it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that Milosevic meant the Albanian policemen who were beating the Serbs at that moment?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it your testimony today that at that moment Albanian policemen were not beating the assembled Serbs?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question. I'm not clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it your testimony today that at that moment Albanian policemen were not beating the assembled Serbs? When I say "Albanian policemen," I'm referring to policemen who were Kosovo Albanians of course.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There wasn't a single ethnically pure group at that time. You cannot claim that they were beating the Serbs. It was a huge meeting where he held a political speech intended to intensify his strategy, to encourage the Serbs that his politics is the right one, that he will look after them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. We're going to move on now. We're going to move on to paragraph 7 of your statement. You say that you had to use the Serbian language. Is it actually correct that younger Albanians, primarily people born after 1970, did not speak or understand the Serbian language?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The majority of the youth born after this year speak the Serbian language.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Here we heard practically from all the younger Albanians who were witnesses that they did not speak or understand the Serbian language. What do you think, were they lying when they said that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I don't know how many younger Albanians we're talking about that testified here. I don't know that they're a representative sample of the majority of younger Albanians. We had mostly witnesses from rural communities, as far as younger Albanians who testified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's a question for argument, Mr. Hannis, how valuable the evidence is, but the question I think has a satisfactory foundation in the evidence we've heard from some younger Albanian people. I think, Mr. Merovci, it would help if you just concentrate on the period shortly after 1970. During that period, I think the suggestion being put to you is that Albanians were not being educated in the Serbian language. Was there a period when that was the case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, this is not the case. This is a time when I was attending secondary school. Serbian language was compulsory subject in secondary education. When I say the majority spoke Serbian, I mean that they understood Serbian and could manage with it. The Serbian language was taught in primary school as well, and it was a compulsory subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm satisfied with that answer, so I will move on to my next topic; although, of course, Mr. Merovci, it is the position of this Defence that Kosovo children did not learn the Serbian language due to the well-known boycott of Serbian schools that were not attended at all by the Albanian children. Do you know that a parallel schooling system had been organised in Kosovo, and was the Serbian language taught at all in these schools?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We're talking about 1970. You have mixed up the time-period. In 1970, the curriculum contained the Serbian language as a compulsory subject, and the Serbian language was a compulsory subject in secondary education as well. Only in higher education you can choose whether you want to do your studies in Albanian or in Serbian. During my time at university, I had subjects that were taught in the Serbian language by Serbian professors, and I actually sit for some exams in the Serbian language. After 1980, when the autonomy was revoked, the Albanians organised themselves and they did not accept the imposed education system by the Serbs. The Albanians organised their own schools and continued their education.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Merovci. I was talking about children born after 1970, so I precisely meant school attendance in the 1980s. You gave us your example, too, but I don't think that you were born after 1970, just like I wasn't. Let us move on. In paragraph 12 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a moment, Mr. Lukic. What did you mean, Mr. Merovci, by saying "after 1980 when the autonomy was revoked?"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: After consulting the colleague, the year was 1989.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, it's a mistake in the transcript. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You're talking about the right to secede and you were asked about that on the 24th of March, 2002, in the Milosevic case. He asked you about after 1992. In your opinion, was there no other way out except for independence? What would you say to us today? After 1992, what was the position of Albanians regarding the independence of Kosovo? You were asked in the Milosevic trial on page 5515.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The stance of the Albanians at the time you are talking was for Kosova to be an independent and neutral state. By "neutral," they implied open to Serbia and Albania. That was a political motto and slogan used by Mr. Rugova for the only reason that we are talking about the time when the former Yugoslavia started to be broken up; and, therefore, the legitimate right of the Kosova people was to organise themselves and they held a referendum in 1991 and the elections in 1992, which were not accepted internationally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We're going to have to break, Mr. Lukic. How are we doing for time?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'll try to calculate that. I'll do my best and I think that I will successfully end before the end of the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. But there will be re-examination, so it may be that we'll try to put in an arrangement for extending in hearing somehow.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'll try and avoid that. I don't know how much my learned friend needs for his --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Haider will speak to both of you when we rise just now and, if necessary, will try to set up an appropriate arrangement. We'll break again, as we have to, Mr. Merovci, for half an hour this time and we'll resume at 10 minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Merovci, at the Milosevic trial on page 5446, line 12 thereof, you say the following: [In English] "Which had been were largely Albanian, most of them left their work refusing the orders brought by Belgrade." [Interpretation] Do you adhere by that statement of yours even today?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. We are talking about the time following the constitutional changes when in the police service these measures, the extraordinary measures, were imposed. Therefore, because of such a policy, Albanians left their jobs en masse. I'm talking only of Albanian policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 16 of your statement, you say that the Albanian policemen stayed with the police if they accepted to be loyal to the Serb regime, that's how they were kept on. What about the LDK, did they issue a proclamation in order to entice Albanians to abandon the police and other state bodies?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall that the LDK has issued such a proclamation. Its stand was that the workers should try as much as they could to keep their work-places and not create -- not give pretexts to be fired. But there was, as I said, an en masse sacking of people or leaving their jobs. But what you are putting to me that only the loyal Albanians were kept cannot be true 100 percent. There may have been some policemen who, for various reasons, personal reasons, has continued to do the same job for some time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that representatives of Serbia spoke on many occasions with Albanian policemen in Kosovo and held many meetings, trying to persuade Albanian policemen, officers, to stay with the police?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know this. If I had known, I might have said. What I know is that Albanians have refused to abide by a policy which was an anti-Albanian policy.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well then. Let me move on to paragraph 19 of your statement. You say here that the only contact you had was with the police, and you speak about the return to Kosovo when Rugova got Sakharov reward in 1988. You said that you were harassed at the border-crossing. Since you travelled a lot, you say that you were often stopped. Were you familiar with any of the police officers who stopped you at the border-crossing and harassed you on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know them personally. They were police in uniforms serving at the border crossing. As I said, from Pristina to the border, we often saw and were stopped by traffic police, but sometimes there were also drafted policemen not part of the traffic teams.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the commander of the traffic police, now that you've mentioned it, in Pristina was Mujo Kujovic, who was a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember this, and I don't know the names of the police -- senior policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 20, when you speak about the interview in May 1995, the time when you were questioned by the state security, you say that you were questioned about the alleged plan by the Albanians to form a shadow Ministry of the Interior. You go on to say: "I was aware of the attempts to create a shadow ministry and that these efforts were led by Dr. Bujar Bukoshi." In other words, we can conclude that at that moment the parallel police force formation was underway in Kosovo, and I'm speaking about May 1995. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We are talking about the government that operated in exile with Mr. Bukoshi, Bujar Bukoshi, being its prime minister. To my knowledge, some efforts were made to set up its structures, as I stated in my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 25, you say that you refused to cooperate with the Serb authorities. The reason was that your only home in case you did would have been a cemetery. Who were you afraid of? Who did you think might have killed you, should you have accepted to cooperate with the Serb authorities?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not as you put it, not the right context. I didn't refuse out of fear, but the meaning is -- here is that before I accept this, I better die.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well then. Let's go to paragraph 28. You say that among the LDK leaders, only Fehmi Agani had some contacts with the KLA to your knowledge. Do you know anything about the possible cooperation between Agani and the KLA, what was it about?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not something concrete, but what I know and have stated is that there was an indirect communication through some activists of the LDK with Mr. Agani, but I cannot be accurate as to the names of such people. It was something which I heard, knew of. When we talk of Mr. Agani, we are talking about a very close collaborator of Mr. Rugova.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How did KLA treat the policies of the LDK and Rugova himself? Were there any threats issued?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what I remember up to now - and now I recall Mr. Rugova's testimony given in this very chair - at no moment, neither orally or in writing, has the KLA ever issued any threats against Mr. Rugova.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the case that took place in September 1998 when the KLA in Cicavica arrested a group of politicians very close to Dr. Rugova, among them was Bleta Pula, Gjergj Dedaj, and others.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know of what you said, and another counsel asked me before. And I said that this group was in communication with the KLA with reference to what you are say ago, and then publicly they refuted such statements; that is, there are five news conference given by these very people. And I remember that they said that everything was done in the context of good communication, something which they publicly acknowledged.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the organisation called FARK, and what was the relationship between this FARK and the KLA?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I know I know from what I have read from the print media. I was not involved in anything, and I didn't possess any relevant information. Therefore, from what I knew and I know, I'm not in a position to give you an authoritative answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move on to paragraph 38. And let me just ask you briefly, since yesterday on page 19, line 15, you commented upon the Milosevic-Holbrooke plan, and this was on LiveNote, page 19. Is it true that you actually never saw this plan?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never saw it personally, and I can say that most of Rugova's associates didn't see it. It was more a plan that was commented upon by the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We may then conclude that you don't know what it contains and what actions would have been violated by that plan -- what would be the violations based on that plan?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's true that I didn't know them in detail, but what I knew and was commented by many and also by Mr. Rugova was the withdrawal of troops from the ground. And this is what I said also in my statement and in my testimony, then I -- as I said, I made a visit about which I spoke about earlier. So I made my statement in this context.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move on to paragraph 42 of your statement. You say: "At the border we could see all of the vehicles and personnel of the Kosovo Verification Mission leaving Kosovo. There were also large numbers of Albanians leaving as well in all sorts of civilian vehicles." Just for the transcript, all of this took place before the bombing started. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. All kilometres of roads were filled with people waiting to cross the car, people -- representatives of various organisations like the OSCE and the verification mission, but as I said there were also civilians in their cars. When we went to Pristina, the situation was terrible. Panic reigned everywhere among people. As to what was going to happen, they were terror-struck as a result of the paramilitaries who were stationed in different places, as I said, yesterday, in the Grand Hotel being one of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would also like to ask you this. Did you hear that on the 21st of March, 1999, at 6.15 in the afternoon in the street of Miladin Popovic in front of the house number 1 to 9 in the neighbourhood of Grmija, there was a traffic patrol which attempted to stop an Audi car and this patrol was attacked and four policemen were killed on that occasion. At that time, you were already in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't remember that, because you are talking about a day when we didn't have proper information about, and we were faced with problems of food supply and a panic situation, as I said, reigning among the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So it is possible then that you may have been in Pristina and that you did not know what was going on in the town because of the situation that prevailed at the time? Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 45, you say that after the 21st of March, nobody went to work and all the services stopped functioning. Up to then, everybody went to work, up to that date. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is partially so. This was a process. The 21st is a day when I returned and I mentioned this date because I was an eye-witness to that, but, as I said, this was an ongoing process.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 46, you speak about the killings of some prominent Albanians. Can we then agree that you did not see Bajram Kelmendi and his two sons being killed and their -- and also that you didn't see the killing of Agim Hajrizi and Latif Berisha. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see the actual murder act. Nobody did for that matter. They only saw the corpses. But the act of murder of Agim Hajrizi was seen by other people, but not by me personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you hear that they had actually been killed by members of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They were not killed by the KLA, and this is very immoral to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you - and I'm not talking about the mortality of my words and I'm not calling for your judgement of my words - I'm just asking you to answer my question. In paragraph 49, you speak about the Serb who was charged with taking you to the apartment where you were to pick up something. You say that he wasn't wearing a uniform but that he was armed. Are you aware of the fact that he was a reservist affiliated with the state security? And, as we all know, those people do not wear uniforms.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was dressed in plain clothes. There is no way how I can know what he was doing, as you are saying he was a reservist. I know that he was armed and he was the man who escorted me up to my apartment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said that Ljubo Joksic from the state security was in charge of this operation. It is to be assumed that he had his men who participated in that. Would that be acceptable by you?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say that Mr. Joksic was what you are alleging him to be. I was the man who simply expressed my opinion that he was a contact person, and there were some other men dressed in civilian clothes who later followed my moves, accompanied me in my moves to the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 50, you say that from the 24th of March, when the bombing started, until the 29th of March, you would drive to Dr. Rugova's house every day at around 11.00, which means that you went by car. What is the distance between your house and Dr. Rugova's house?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is about three kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You've mentioned Jankovic from Suva Reka. Let us just clarify this. Did he say that he worked in Suva Reka or that he hailed from Suva Reka and worked in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I may say what he himself told me at that moment, and this is what he told me: "I'm Major Jankovic from Suva Reka." I couldn't ask any further questions of him because, as I said, the situation was difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When the policemen entered Dr. Rugova's house where you were at the time, did they try to chase you out of the house?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Initially, it was the soldiers who came first. They broke down both doors. When they broke down the second door, I came down from the upper floor from where I was seeing what was going on, hoping to calm them down and not be as aggressive as I saw them being from the window with other neighbours. And they maltreated me. When I introduced myself, telling them that there are people here, there are women and children, and Mr. Rugova lives here, then they said, "We came to do our job." And this is where the man who asked for NATO lives. I cannot say at this moment they tried to chase us out, but they consulted their other people because the situation was calm and this situation after that lasted for many hours. To put it briefly, initially, I didn't see any tendency to drive us out of our home immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you also know that Mr. Agim Hajrizi, who was in the limelight as a politician and he was very close to the KLA, was able to walk freely around Pristina throughout the war?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know this. And the policemen themselves told me that he and his sister were walking around the streets of the town and they described him -- people described him as the Mandela of the Balkans.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 54, you say that during the night, that is to say after the 31st of March, fire was opened by the Serb forces. Do you remember that on the 3rd of April, 1999, Abdullah Hajrullaha, an Albanian, tried to enter Dr. Rugova's house with a weapon in his hands and in order to stop him from doing that the police had to use fire-arms?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time we were told by the police about what you're saying. The police did not mention any names, but only the attempt. However, after some time after the war, things came on to surface, things were made public, and it was discovered that it was Mr. Hajrush Abdullahu who was a driver of Mr. Rugova. And this could not be as an -- understood as a person who came to attack Mr. Rugova, rather than like a person who came to save Mr. Rugova or evacuate him. This is what I know and what I learned also from his family members.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You know that on that occasion he had been armed and that he tried to jump over the fence, right?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. I'm only telling you that I was told that someone is trying to attack, to carry out an attack. This was said by the police at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you would go out of Dr. Rugova's house, either when you went to Belgrade or when you moved about Pristina, were you protected by policemen wearing civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the beginning it was uniformed policemen. On the first occasion, there were four policemen; on the second occasion, there were two policemen; and later on I was escorted only by persons in civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. My next question. Perhaps you've already answered, but I'm going to ask nevertheless so that it would not remain just hanging in the air. Do you know that threats were addressed to Dr. Rugova from Adem Demaci's office by telephone?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, this is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On page 5516, Mr. Milosevic asked you whether you knew Mr. Tanic and whether anyone from your party, Rugova or some other Albanian, negotiated with Mr. Tanic. You said, "I personally never met Tanic and I don't think that any one of us met him." Even after 2002, up to the present day, do you still stand by that?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I still stand by that. I do not know this person.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would just like to ask you something else. Did it ever happen that you reported harassment that you were subjected to, for example, in 1998 at the time when the Kosovo Verification Mission was in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not clear what kind of harassment you are referring to. Can you clarify, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I am referring to mistreatment at the border or by traffic police. Did you report that kind of maltreatment to anyone in the Kosovo Verification Mission or to any of the police officers?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police itself harassed us. It is natural that -- it is not natural to report harassment to the person that harasses you. However, we did write about this harassment in press releases and public statements, and we distributed these releases and statements in the entire world.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you just, please, tell us where we could find these reports, please.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can find information on these harassments in the materials of the Kosova press centre. I don't know if they still exist and can be found on the web page. I don't know what is the status with the archives.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you, Mr. Merovci. I have no further questions, and I believe that we are going to fit into our regular sitting hours and that we will finish today. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That remark puts the pressure on me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Merovci --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, there's an element of flexibility because there's no case this afternoon, I leave it to you to do your best.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think I can do it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Merovci, yesterday Mr. O'Sullivan was asking you some questions about the meeting on the 28th of April, 1999, and played the videotape for you. I want to ask you some questions surrounding that meeting and that videotape. As of the 28th of April, I understand that you and Mr. Rugova had been under house arrest for four weeks up to that point. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. From 31st of March to 5th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how did you and Mr. Rugova get to this meeting? Did you drive on your own or did someone take you there?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: They communicated this meeting to us. We were not in a position to refuse to attend this meeting, and with their cars we were taken to this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Who took you there? Who physically took you there?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The person who invited us and accompanied us in the cars was Mr. Ljubo Joksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: From the DB?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Who took you back to Dr. Rugova's house after the meeting?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the same way, by the same cars, and by the same person, Mr. Joksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And while you were at the meeting, did Dr. Rugova's wife and family remain behind at the house, guarded by police?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: At the meeting, was there any police or soldiers present?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were always present, but at a later stage they were mainly in civilian clothes but armed, even at a press conference in an interview that I gave there was police presence. There were also uniformed persons with long-barrel weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I want to go to Exhibit 1D60, Your Honour. And this was the videotape of that meeting that Mr. O'Sullivan played, and I just want to go to a brief clip. I think it begins at 3 minutes and 33 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, Mr. Merovci, I want you to have a look. We've got a still shot. This shows apparently some of the cameramen that were present during this press conference. Can you tell me what the man on the right is wearing in that photograph, if you can see.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was a shirt, a military shirt, a uniform, camouflage pattern and he put on a vest to look as if he was a journalist.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. At this meeting, Mr. Rugova's speech is shown on the tape and he said: "Our main goal is to get out of this present situation." He could have been speaking about your house arrest as well as --

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour, this calls for speculation and supposition. It's has no probative value the way it's phrased.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's leading as well the way it's phrased, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. I'll withdraw that and move on to another topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Fila asked you today about the emergency measures or the extraordinary measures. In your statement, in paragraph 13, you refer to the badges that Albanian employees were required -- were being asked to wear to come into the bank. Can you tell us in the Serbian language what words actually appeared on those badges so we can hear the translation into English.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Up to this time, we had our usual bank badges. Mine was with my photograph written in Albanian, my name and the code. With the introduction of the violent measures in the bank, the communication language was the Serbian language and the Cyrillic alphabet. "Organi Presili Mera;" Organs of Coercive Measures was the title.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So when you use the word "coercive measures," you're referring to the exact words that were on the badges that you were given at the bank?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Fila also asked about your conversation with Mr. Sainovic when you were asking to be allowed to go abroad, and he said you were free to go but he couldn't guarantee your security. At page 33 today, lines 16 to 19, I think you said that you understood that that was addressed to you personally. What about Dr. Rugova, do you know if he was free to go?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one was free to go, but what we are talking about refers to my trip to Skopje, and on this occasion Mr. Sainovic expressed his security concerns regarding my security. But this was a pretext in order to prevent our leaving Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm not clear on that. Was this the only time that Mr. Sainovic expressed that you were free to go but he couldn't guarantee your security? Was it only one time and in connection with your trip to Skopje?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my recollection, we spoke of this subject only on this one occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, at paragraph 74, Mr. -- Mr. Fila was asking you today, I think at page 34, line 22, about Mr. Sainovic's role in all of this and whether you viewed it of him being more of a messenger or an envoy. At paragraph 74, you say that Mr. Sainovic asked if the police who were guarding you were behaving properly and that if they weren't he would rectify that. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall that. This came after a few days after our isolation and after the meeting with Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how was Mr. Sainovic treated by the police who were guarding you during his several visits when they came to see you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't see where this re-direct comes from. What is it that I asked about the police and Sainovic so that the Prosecutor has to re-examine on that? What the Prosecutor is doing now is examination-in-chief. There are no grounds otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it has to do with his role.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Fila, the point that you made was what Sainovic's role was and suggested he was a messenger or an envoy, and that raises an issue that the Prosecutor is entitled to explore. So we will allow him to do that and repel the objection. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Merovci, do you recall my question? How was he treated by the police?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: He behaved in a normal way, came and went. He had an armed person who accompanied him. I could not tell if there was any unusual conduct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did they treat him differently or the same as any of the other people who came to visit you during those weeks of house arrest?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was treated as a person who was, in a way, at the head of a mission. He was treated as a senior person. He was treated not in the same way as other people who came to visit us as journalists or the Russian ambassador.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no other questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I apologise. [Interpretation] Just with regard to the transcript, Your Honour, by your leave. We have redacted the necessary pages. So in line with that in relation to the 23rd of May, 2002, which is D580, we would single out 54 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the page numbers please be repeated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you give us the numbers again, Mr. Cepic, the interpreter has missed them.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. 5452, it is one page; 5469; and 5470.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: About 24th of May, 2002, pages number 5483, 5484, 5489 from 89 to 5491; and then 5496, 5497, 54 -- from 5499 to 5510. Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no objection to that if I may have leave to review it and see if I want to propose additional pages to put something in context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think what we should do is reserve a decision on this until tomorrow and you should tell us then.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Merovci, I hope that we've completed the exercise at a satisfactory time for you and that you can catch appropriate transport home. That does now conclude your evidence. Thank you very much for coming back to the Tribunal to give it, or rather, for coming to the Tribunal to give it. And it will be of assistance to us in our deliberations. You are now free to leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, one matter in relation to tomorrow's witness. The notification of the accompanying documents says this: "The Prosecution will be seeking to have portions of testimony of the witness from the Milosevic trial admitted, as there are some portions in private session, there's a public version and a version which the Prosecution will be seeking to have admitted under seal," and you then give the two numbers. What I actually have received is a very large transcript because I think it covers three days.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: More than that, Your Honour, I think it covers seven days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's seven in fact. Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It's not the entire transcript. It's excerpts of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That is the redacted version we have, is it? Or at least it's restricted to what you want to rely on; it's not the whole transcript?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour, not at all because he testifies about Bosnia, Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Indeed. And the one that has been sent, is it the one which includes the private session evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, Exhibit 2590 is the one that includes everything, including everything the portions that we want under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: 2589 is the open sessions only.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So it is the full version, right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I should say Exhibit 2600 is the one that we propose to have filed publicly. It has the redactions. Oh, I'm sorry, I misspoke, that's the statement, my apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Very well, we shall adjourn now and resume at 9.00 tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 18th day of January, 2007, at 9.00 a.m.
